newsitem.title: USA: NYS Senate urges Assembly to approve budget reform.
newsitem.headline: NYS Senate urges Assembly to approve budget reform.

text.p: Saying he feared New York state was at risk of again failing to approve its budget on time, the Senate on Tuesday called upon the Assembly to reconvene before the elections to approve budget reform.

Gov. George Pataki, who held the 1997 fiscal budget hostage to pressure the legislature to agree to proposals on other issues, like workers' compensation, expects to call a special legislative session after the November 5 elections.
The special session is needed to deal with the sweeping changes mandated by the new federal welfare bill.
A spokesman for the Assembly Leader, Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, was not immediately available to comment.
The state, whose 1997 fiscal budget is due on April 1, did not finally reach a deal year until 104 days after it was due, setting a new national record for late budgets.

Rating agencies harshly criticized the delays, saying they did not reflect sound fiscal management. And New York's public schools were forced to take out nearly $500 million in costly, short-term loans while they waited for a budget to be reached.
"We increase the costs to everybody with delay, with uncertainity. It's wasteful, it's inefficient, it's not good government," Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, D-Troy, told reporters in Albany.
He added that he thought the Senate should evalaute a proposal by the State Education Commissioner, who has said the legislature should consider a bond act to raise funds to upgrade public schools.
The Senate Majority Leader is not alone is his campaign to improve the budget process, as both Pataki, a Republican, and the state comptroller, H. Carl McCall, a Democrat, have urged reforms.

But it was not clear whether Gov. George Pataki, who has said he felt legislators would be too distracted to consider welfare reform until after the elections, now would join Bruno in asking the Assembly to meet before then.
A spokeswoman for Pataki said only "We welcome any effort made to reform the current budget process."

The Senate Majority Leader, who denied that he was using budget reform as a campaign issue, said that there were "plenty of excuses" for why the 1998 fiscal budget might be delayed. He pointed to uncertainity over welfare reform, saying he was hearing the impact could range from a $250 million surplus to a $1 billion deficit.

McCall has estimated that the new federal plan, which replaces the Aid to Families with Dependent Children program with one called Temporary Assistance to Needy Families, could create a surplus of up to $300 million in the first year.

While the program being replaced is the main federal cash welfare program, New York state is particularly vulnerable under the new federal rules, which impose strict restrictions on the aid that legal immigrants can collect, because New York City has as many as 400,000 illegal and undocumented aliens.
